utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties had a preliminary matter or even more to raise. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just to let you know that these videos, D245 and 246, that we received from the Defence yesterday, we've looked at them and can't really make out enough of them to be able to stipulate to anything, but perhaps some more coffee and more discussions we might be able to deal with that. But right now, we would still be objecting. And on your question yesterday regarding the position on the Defence's request to certify the ruling on the five days. The Prosecution take no position on that and if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No response. Therefore, then the Chamber will decide on the motion seeking a certificate for an appeal. We hope to hear, then, from the parties immediately after the recess about D245 and D246. Mr. Lukic, any matter you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just briefly. We missed one deadline on the 16th of July this year in regard of the 27th 92 bis motion. On the same day we had to file 24th and 25th 92 bis motions, and somehow we missed one, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we kindly ask for an additional seven days from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven days. Any objection by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, absolutely. We occasionally miss a deadline ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request is granted. You have seven additional days to count from today? Yes. So not from the original deadline, the 16th, but as of today, which is the 26th plus seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter? If not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The -- is there an estimate about the time the Defence would need for their further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I still am at about an hour to potentially an hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if we look at the estimates, one hour and ten minutes would the -- would be the ultimate moment. Good morning, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Ivetic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you in relation to the work that you did in generating the list of missing persons relative to Srebrenica, did you take any steps to verify either the ICRC or PHR lists with any existing official registers of births and registers of death that were kept by the official authorities?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because -- no. Yes and no. There's no electronic birth or death register for Bosnia. So that wouldn't have been possible. We did check with the census 1991 which is the most solid source of population data for a country like Bosnia. As I explained yesterday, the two entities started assembling an electronic database in the -- several years later on the initiative of the Tribunal, and these data were then compared with the ICRC list without finding any. They had very few -- they had very few data on Srebrenica-related deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you've mentioned the 1991 census. Am I correct that the census-taking activities of the state census organs in 1991 continued right up to the outbreak of the war, I believe, until 31 March 1991?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data were collected in April 1991 for all of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, and referring to the so-called census date of 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, thus, the results of this 1991 census had not been subjected to the types of verification and correction procedures which normally would be conducted for -- for censuses. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm not -- I'm not sure exactly what they did, but we discovered after we received the census file -- excuse me, that there were numerous errors in spelling of names and probably other mistakes as well. So you are correct, it had not gone through that regular checking and, say, correction on names, but names are not statistically interesting anyway, so they might not have done it. What is done in many countries is that after the main census has been taken, there is a post-enumeration survey with -- is taken then of, say, 1 per cent of the population, so one per cent of the enumerators are interviewed again, and then the data from the sample survey and the full census are compared to check the quality of the data. This was not done. I don't know if it was planned or dropped because much the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your review of the ICRC list against the 1991 census, am I correct that you found up to 13 per cent of the names on the ICRC list that did not seem to exist on the 1991 census; that is, they could not be located under that biographical data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what we wrote in our report, yes. But that doesn't mean that those people were not enumerated in 1991. The reason we did not find those 13 per cent could be due to false in the spelling of the names that we had not discovered and corrected, lacking or wrong date of birth, et cetera. It could also be that some of the missing were not enumerated in 1991 because they lived in other republics or abroad. Anyway, I think we found 87 per cent which is an extremely high percentage, so we are very pleased that we found this high proportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what proportion of the PHR list were you able to identify positively and match to persons listed in the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not do specific match of the PHR with the 1991 census. The PHR list was integrated with the ICRC list in what we call the OTP lists of missing and dead persons, which were produced in the year 2000, 2005, and 2009. And they were less than 200 additional persons in the PHR which were not in the various ICRC lists. So it was a small additional number. We did not see any sense in making a special comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to look at something contained in one of your earlier reports. If we can call up 65 ter number 4510. And it is page 6 in the English, page 7 in the B/C/S. And I'd like to look at the second paragraph from the top in the English. And, sir, here, you are talking and you say: "The survival of some people may not have been reported to ICRC, for example, because they did [sic] not want their survivorship to be disclosed." Now I'd like to know here, are you referring to the persons who had been listed as missing or dead and who actually had survived when you say "they did not want their survivorship to be disclosed."

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it's a hypothetical thesis that there may have been some people who did not report their survival to ICRC in spite of their being on the missing list, but we have not come across any such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to the start of the -- of the hostilities in July of 1995, the attack on Srebrenica is said to have begun the 6th of July, 1995, and lasted until 11 July 1995. Do you know the exact number of casualties on the side of the Bosnian Muslim defenders of Srebrenica that would have died during this time-period of 6 July to 11 July 1995 in any fighting that was under way?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not been given that information. Moreover, I don't know if those being killed in that period were reported as missing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at 1D1153 with you in e-court. And the same should not be broadcast to the public as it contains identifying information from ICMP. And while we wait for that to come up, sir, I can tell you this is a chart that resulted from the work of a Defence demographer, Ms. Svetlana Radovanovic. First of all, am I correct that you are familiar with this individual Ms. Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met her here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now looking at the document, first of all, I can tell you that the right side of the table concerns identifications by ICMP pursuant to DNA analysis and indicates for those what mass grave in the Srebrenica area they were exhumed from. The middle column that says "spisak armije BiH" reflects the unverified information from the armija of BiH, as I understand it, of their records of when these men, their soldiers, would have become deceased or gone missing and, of course, the left side of the column is the information I believe from one of the lists that that you and your colleagues would have prepared for the persons on your missing list, and there is the column that indicate the information that you had about the suspected date of death of these individuals. And, as you can see, the men on this list, at least, all have dates reported by the army records as being predating 11 July 1995, sometimes even a few years before. And I believe this -- this -- this is the result of efforts done in 2008, so it's definitely material that would not have been in your possession when you were doing your initial reports. But I want to ask you, if this information is verified - and I believe this document has 125-odd individuals for whom this information is available - but would -- if this information is verified, would that raise questions in your mind about the reliability of the information that you had from the various sources that you used to put the men in your report as having been missing following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say that this was presented in the trial against Blagojevic, I believe, which was then in 2001 or -2 or something. I don't quite remember. There were -- we received lists from the Bosnian army about the number of people who had been army soldiers who had been killed, and we then -- the Tribunal then asked the Ministry of Defence in Sarajevo to check inconsistent dates as here when the dates of missing persons were found to be before 11th of July. And the date was changed and corrected by the Ministry of Defence, I believe, in 127 cases. This can be found in the 2009 report. Because it turned out that the -- the army records regarding the date of death was rather sloppy. So there was also no information on the place of death. So I, of course, do not know that particular name, but we need -- I would need to check whether that name -- that date remains standing or whether it was changed by the Ministry of Defence. There were, I think, there were 38 outstanding cases that were also requested -- the OTP requested the Ministry of Defence to look into. I do not know whether we had any response to that request.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To just make it short, do I understand that most of the data provided turned out to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So to some extent the verification which was at the beginning of the question of Mr. Ivetic had been done to some extent and showed that in many cases the data were not verified and were not accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. If you like, I could check this closer in the break in the year 2009 report. Or now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would do it in the break and give us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further details --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- such as whether it's -- the date of death, whether that, for example, was corrected or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also whether it then, after the correction, was then within the time-frame of July 1995 or at any earlier date because if the 10th of January of 1994 is a wrong date, it could still be -- the 1st of January of that year or what Mr. Ivetic is interested in, to see whether it -- the -- the verified date of death is outside the scope of the July events in 1995. Further, Mr. Ivetic, I see a large number of persons having been reported to be dead on the 10th of January, 1994. I do not know whether there is any event related to that. That's maybe an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and that's why I've always said unverified because I think there does need to be more follow-up done on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although part of it apparently has been done --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- already.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, let me switch gears slightly -- and we can remove this document now so we don't have to worry about the broadcasting of the same. The UNHCR, did you try to gain access to their records and information as to refugees to try and improve your work on the reports that you did?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But the UNHCR is very protective about their data, so we did not get any data on individuals from UNHCR. I was not even allowed to visit their office in Sarajevo because of -- they wanted to be absolutely certain, sure about their neutrality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, am I correct that you also personally urged and tried to get the office of high representative and other officials in Bosnia and Herzegovina to organise conduct an appropriate census not only for Srebrenica but for the rest of the two entities?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, sir. I wrote that in my report that it would be very useful to have a new full census of Bosnia since the previous one was in 1991. When I was active in this work, this was already almost ten years ago, I'm now -- it is more than 20 years ago, but now there are specific plans for a new census, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to look at 1D1166 with you. And if we can have page 52 in e-court. That should correlate to transcript page 7013 of the Popovic proceedings. And if we look at the part from line 7 through 25, and there's a couple of sources identified there. I guess I'll just read it. It will be perhaps the quickest way. "Q. All right. Well I guess" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. If we can -- if we can scroll down I can see where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's the wrong page. This is 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's going be to the wrong transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Anyway, let me rephrase the questions like this, sir. Am I correct that as part of your work you also did not refer to work done on the 1991 census by either the Sarajevo or the Banja Luka authorities? They both did work and, I think, up to -- well, at least 2003 to try and create some additional information about the census. Was that part of your review?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, of course, look at the work done in the federal institute in Sarajevo, and I also met with representatives of the statistical office in Banja Luka. But I did not become aware of any further work that they did that would have any influence on our work on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now call up 1D1163 and page 45 of that document. And that should correlate to transcript page 7110. I see we're on the same page. And if we could zoom in on the bottom two lines and this will bleed on to the following page. I'd like to go through some testimony that you gave in that case in relation to --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, which case was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was the Blagojevic case. And then I'll have some follow-up questions for you so if could you please follow along and keep in kind whether in fact the testimony as recorded appears to comport with your recollections and knowledge. So beginning at line 24: "Q. Could you tell us: How did you arrive at this conclusion that all of the men, you know, as you indicate: 'All the [sic] men are included in the estimate of missing persons, but hardly any of them -- any of the men were combatants.' How did you arrive at that. "A. Because I learned through reading, talking to people, seeing videos that that was the case, that there were few combatants at the time they were killed. I know there were armed people who were taken prisoners on their way when they crossed the road at Nova Kasaba, for instance, and later executed. The number of men who were actually combatants, I don't know. But hardly any, perhaps that is a bit too strong. "Q. Okay. Well, I wouldn't say 'strong' I would say inaccurate. Would you fight me on that one? "A. I agree. I could agree that that is inaccurate. On the other hand, a large number of men were not combatants in that group. "Q. You talked about the age bracket of 16 to 60 as being combatants. Correct? "A. Yes. "Q. Okay. And based on your figures, it would appear that the range of men that went missing are within that range, more or less? "A. Yes." And I'd like to ask you, sir, first of all, the section that we've read, does it comport to your recollection as accurately depicting your knowledge and the way you would answer these questions today?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I think I learned more. I don't think I would say hardly any. But also in the Blagojevic trial, I said perhaps that is a bit too strong and I stand by that. It was a bit too strong or inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: But nobody knows how many people were actually killed while fighting on their way through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question for you in relation to this selection that we've read is that, first of all, you talk about videos that you looked at, and I want to know what was the purpose in relation to your demographic review of viewing these videos that you have made reference to.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to gain general background knowledge about the situation in Srebrenica on the 11 July 1995 and later. Since, at that time, I had never been there, I didn't know the -- what the scenery was like, was it very steep or hilly or -- it was useful to get an impression of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were these videos items which the Office of the Prosecutor selected for you to review?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- the one I saw, perhaps the only one, was the BBC Panorama and I learned about this -- these videos in various contexts and asked -- and knew the OTP had copies, and I asked if I could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to talk about another source of information which you identify in your reports as having reviewed. The Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. First of all, am I correct that we are talking about the organisation which was headed by a Mr. Amor Macovic?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to this secondary source of information, how did you rate the confidence level of the information that you received from them?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, we don't have information on the precise confidence level in a statistical sense, so I cannot -- I could not rate that. But the kind -- I don't remember what kind of information we received from Mr. Macovic, if we received any at all. I don't think there was any information that we used directly in creating the OTP list of missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps use his information or verify or double-check information that was already existing on your OTP list of missing?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't recall because -- and if he had received any, we would have, of course, double-checked. But I'm not sure we received any data on individuals I mean, and now I recall meeting Mr. Macovic and asking for data on individuals on the deaths but I am -- I don't recall receiving any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough then. Then I'd like to move to another item. Back when we were looking at your CV yesterday, there was a reference in there to your having chaired a review committee for some work done by a Patrick Ball, and there's a reference in some of your reports to relying on a method employed by Ball and others. Are we talking about the same Patrick Ball in both instances?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is Patrick Ball someone who is likewise engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor to perform demographic and statistical expertise at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he has ever been employed here, but he has testified on some occasions about refugee flows out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could take a look specifically at 65 ter number 5308, this would, I believe, be your 2003 addendum report, and if we can have page 5 in both versions up on the screen. And I'd like to go through with you on -- there is the reference in number 3 that reads as follows: "Fully 5.712, or 76 per cent, of the missing persons were found on both lists of missing persons, i.e., the ICRC and PHR lists. This information can be used to estimate the likely total number of people who went missing, whether reported or not, using a method called the capture-tag-recapture technique or multiple systems estimation (Sekar and Deming 1949; Marks Seltzer and Krotki 1974; Bishop Fienberg and Holland 1975). This method has been used widely in population statistics but it has also been used to make estimates for other species such as fish." And now the footnote here in number 3 for this method being used widely in population statistics refers to a recent example which we can see at the on the bottom -- yes, it's visible on the bottom of the screen. A recent example included Ball et al 2002 which was presented as evidence in the trial against Slobodan Milosevic. Sir, is this a reference to the work that we were just discussing of Mr. Patrick Ball in relation to the Kosovo case?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. But since I don't have that report with me I cannot be absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, has Mr. Ball's work been widely accepted in the demographic and statistics communities as being an appropriate application of the multiple systems estimation or capture-tag-recapture technique as it relates to population statistics?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ball is a extant statistician. He has worked on humanitarian analysis work both in Latin America and on Kosovo and his work is highly regarded [realtime transcript read in error "recorded"].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, how significant is Mr. Ball's work to the overall findings of your report or at least this addendum in particular that cites to it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did -- he did not work on the same -- on Bosnia. So I would say the findings are -- his findings do not relate to my work on Bosnia. But if you refer to the methodology which he made me aware of but which was, when known -- had been used many times in many countries, what I found -- found using this capture recapture method, I did only marginal -- marginally. It did not contribute very much to the total number and we never used the new estimate for anything. I think one of the reasons why it was only a marginal improvement or an adding up of numbers was that the two samples were not independent of the two populations. The PHR list and ICRC lists were not created independently which is a basic assumption in this literature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at page 15, line 24, I think I heard the witness say that the work of Ball he referred to is highly "regarded" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rather than "recorded."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I -- I tend to agree. I think that was what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness does not contradict it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to just briefly review with you two findings of the Milutinovic Trial Chamber as to Mr. Ball and his work from the Trial Judgement in that case to get your comment on that. If we can have 1D1172 in e-court and I'm told page 14 in both versions. Both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness has told us that he hasn't used the technique or the system by Mr. Ball. So, therefore, I wonder what the relevance is of going through perhaps comments or even not accepting that work which was not used by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You may be right. Let me rephrase the question that I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just ask you, sir, you say that he is highly -- that Mr. Ball is highly regarded in the community. Are you aware that he was disregarded and explicitly the Chamber found not to rely upon him in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That -- again, the same problem is that if this witness did not rely on any of his work, then who criticised him, whether it was the Trial Chamber or whomever seems to lose most if not all of its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honour, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about the group entitled MAG, or Muslims Against Genocide, which I think you also cite in your subsequent -- your later reports, I should say, as a source that was looked at. First of all, sir, do you have knowledge of the methodology used by this group in gathering information for the Bosnian book of the dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I visited them in Sarajevo at least once and saw how they worked and how they collected information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, then, in terms of how they collected information, would they have collected information from similar sources, i.e., from relatives, that the PHR and the ICRC lists also did, according to their methodology?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they also used -- they used all kinds of public information. They didn't have access to any non-public information as far as I know. But in addition to, that they used all kinds of newspaper reports, interviews from families, neighbours, and others, so they used everything they came across and probably of varying quality. And I think they had problems comparing the information from various sources about the same person. And they didn't -- not have a systematic way of doing that. I -- as far as I recall, they kept only the -- the most reliable piece of information but the source of the information for each person was unclear, if they had several sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the work of that group took any efforts to differentiate between missing combatants and missing civilians?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look just briefly at one of your reports, number 5309, in e-court. And page 3 in both languages. And if we could focus on the middle of the page, the matching rate for MAG and it's recorded here if I'm reading this correctly, and that's what I want to ask you is, am I reading this correctly to say that 76 per cent of the records from the Muslims Against Genocide database could be matched to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this says in the report, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So that is the correct reading of that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, stepping back from these other organisations that you either got information from or tried to get information from, I want to talk now a little bit about your work. And is it correct that you developed 71 rules or criteria keys to try to link missing persons with the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps more. And a list of these criteria is given in -- in the 2009 report. I think it may be useful to look at that, if I can find it in -- yes, on page 81 in the English version of the 2009 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you say it's perhaps more. Okay, I understood now. Would you agree that each of these keys, whether 71 or more, represents a relaxing of what would be called the unique key; that is, the combination of the following information: Name, last name, father's name, date of birth, and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, would it be possible to have that on the board so we can relate to what the factors are as addressed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Have what on the board? My question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The -- just the list --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- on page 88 of the factors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 81 .

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. If we can have the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking to find the number of the 2009 report. I believe that's ... is that the integrated report? There were several 2009 reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 11270. Sorry, I think it's 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 269 is what I've got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 269 is the right number. Integrated report, 65 ter 11269. In the English version, the 71 items can be found on pages 81 and 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, now, sir, I'll -- I'll -- to be fair I will repeat the question for you. Would you agree that each of these 71 criteria or keys represents a relaxing of the so-called unique key which would be a combination of the following information: Name, last name, father's name, date of birth, and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would use that terminology that, but it's okay. But if you look at the screen, you will see that when we do use the -- the following criteria: First name, father's name, last name, date of birth, place of death, then we get the -- we got 3.325 matches, which is almost half of the -- on the total list. But then since there's so many misprints and missing data in all the lists we looked at, we, as you said, relaxed information. We used only in the initial of the first name and otherwise similar to the first matching criterion and we got 257. And that it could be that the name that was recorded in one of the lists, say, ICRC list, the first name, sort of a nickname was used or that there was a misprint in the nickname. So that's how it did not -- that match did not come up in the first round. However, we did not accept these matches without consulting and comparing other pieces of information like place of birth -- and date of birth was there, of course, but place of birth and other available information to see if he -- if it was likely that these 255 matches concerned the same persons. And so we did that, trying -- trying to be imaginative and tried different criteria. This is a methodology called fuzzy matching. If you don't have exact data, we need to do fuzzy matching and try out different things. In some countries, like my own in Norway, we only use one criteria for matching data from various sources and that is the personal identification number. But that number in the former Yugoslavia was not used by everybody and there was -- there were many errors in the lists that we had available where that number was, so we had to use other -- we had to use name and other kinds of information. In modern matching techniques there are now, I've learned, methods that apply probabilities to matches. We don't -- when I started doing this work I wasn't aware of this methodology and also in -- in legal cases you cannot really rely on probabilities because you need to be absolutely certain. I don't think the Court would have been satisfied with -- say with there's an 80 per cent probability that this person is the same in the ICRC lists and in the census, for example. So that's why we used all this different criteria, I see criterion 22 resulted in 2.078 matches, whereas the two previous criterias did not result in any, and the last criterion number, 71, resulted in one person, as far as I remember. So this is a perfectly valid methodology, but as I -- let me repeat that we always compared and checked whether the matches that came up in less than ideal -- with less than ideal criteria were highly likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, please check on the transcript before you. Line 17 of the current page. I'm not sure if the number and the other terms are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- yeah. I didn't say "Krajina" at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "That's why we used all ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Criteria," maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] item 22 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, it was I think criterion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was criterion number 22 resulted in 2.078 matches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir. Is it correct that whereas you use these 71 rules for the census, in the case of the voters list if there was incomplete data, the possibility of a match was restricted by imposing an additional condition such as a matching location, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you repeat? As a matching location or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Location of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of -- of -- matching location of either death or disappearance.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no -- in the voters list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Location of the residents or birth?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And ...

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: While you are thinking, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- let me add that there was much less information in the voters list than in the census, so we did not have so much information at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the process of using these 71 rules, in essence, or using this method has no significant limitations that is to say it is possible that anyone, however poor the information on their identity may be, can be found in the census by basically just using this type of fuzzy searching until you reach a positive result for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That -- there's no foundation in that statement given that he's already talked about 13 per cent of people that were not matched in this census, so it makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness would be perfectly able to answer the question. If you want to re-read it, you find it on your screen at this moment. The question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether this system does not allow to always find a match. That's, in short, Mr. Ivetic, I think, what you are telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean, Mr. Ivetic, to always finding a true match or are you indicating that this method could also result in false matches?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The latter.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's always a probability that the match is false but we develop methods to avoid false matches. And as was indicated by the President and by Mr. McCloskey, then the -- we did find 87 per cent match -- matches in the census. The 13 remaining matches -- 13 per cent, that we did not match, could be due to faulty data and lack of data. If we had been less conservative, we could have probably increased that 87 per cent to a higher number, but to be on the safe and cautious side we did not proceed any further. So we would have to do more sort of manual work, visual work, very extremely time-consuming, to receive a higher matching per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification of your question. Are you suggesting in the question that using these 71 criteria becoming vague here and there, that finally you could match Mr. Brunborg to be the same as Mr. McCloskey. Is that more or less, of course, with some exaggeration, what you are suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would say with some exaggeration, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But two totally different persons. Not a name spelt slightly differently but just different names, different dates of birth, et cetera, but if you choose the right criterion that you would find most likely a match anyhow how different the available information would be. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what I -- could you please comment on my layman's understanding of the question, which was confirmed by Mr. Ivetic as -- with some exaggeration to be what he asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, sir, that your understanding is very good. If there were completely different names with all the names - surname, first name, father's name - beginning with different letters, for example, we would never have a match between a person on the missing list and the census list. There has to be some similarity. And, in addition, some background information on, say, place of birth. If we didn't have that, if the place of birth was widely different, then an association or possible match was dropped. We did find many possible matches but they were dropped after closer inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that even if you find similarities but at the same time you find contradicting information on the two persons, that you would drop them and not even further consider them to match?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. If I may mention one interesting example is the example of twins, which are born on the same date, same place, same father's name, same family name, often similar first names, and so if you had one person in the missing list looking almost the same as a pair of twins, we would not -- we could not conclude which of the twins that person -- that matched the missing person, so it was dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've answered all the questions that I had for you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think at the same time that it's time for a break. Mr. Brunborg, we'd like to see you back after 20 minutes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do not have any re-direct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will ask my colleagues whether they have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Only one follow-up to a discussion we had yesterday. The voters list after the war, you told us that you'd checked that list as well and that some people on the missing list were on the voters list. Do you know anything about participation of people on the voters list who, in effect, did take part in the -- in the voting, in the elections?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me see ... I -- I learned that there was a big difference in the -- amongst the ethnic groups. I think we looked at it and found that the Muslims had much higher voting percentage than the Serbs and the Croats. Does that partly answer your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. I --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. I was --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- aiming at a different thing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You -- you had your list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you looked into the list of voters at the first elections after the war. Did you -- and --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you couldn't exclude that those were in fact missing persons?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you checked if they took part -- if any of them --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- if any of them took part in the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I understand your question. Sorry for the misunderstanding. We did not have information on the actual voting. We only had information on those who registered to vote, and of those nine people who registered to vote and at the same time as being on the missing list, the cause of that, we don't know. It could be cheating, it could be faulty registration, some errors. We later learned that two of those nine were actually found to be dead. So for those two there was obviously a mistake, intentional or not, in the registration of voting. It would have been very interesting to know who actually voted as you asked about, but unfortunately we did not have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, before we conclude your examination, Mr. Brunborg, you offered to give us further information about the inaccuracies, I think, you had established in the data of the BiH army, I think it was. People who have -- were reported to have died well before July 1995. Now, if it would take you a few minutes, then we'd just take the break and take your time. If you say, I have it almost immediately available, then we would consider not to take the break and then conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's try to do it right away. On the page 97 on our 2009 report, which is -- I learned is 11269, there's a list -- the beginning of the list of the 220 cases -- perhaps we could have it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's Table 6.4(1).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 97 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Page numbering in -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it should not be broadcast. Or is it a public document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be broadcast to me. Yeah. Thank you. The name that was mentioned by Defence counsel was Mr. Bajic who was believed to be dead, reported by the army to die on the 10th of January, 1994. On page 97, I don't see any Bajic. So it could be that that name -- it's probably occurring further down. Since most of the 127 of those 120 cases, at least 127 were then confirmed to have the wrong date of death, it is quite likely that the same would be the case for Mr. Bajic. But I cannot tell for sure. We'll see that there are -- I can see that there are some other people who reported to have died on the 10th of January, 1994, say, Omerovic at the -- close to the bottom -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If we are -- could you in one way or another refer to the persons without giving their names because that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. So the three names at the bottom of the page are -- have always -- all been reported as dying on the 10th of January, 1994. And several other names. So that was -- whether it was a big battle on that day or whether the army chose to use that date for some reason, I don't know. We would need to check with their response from the army. But as I said, many were changed, and there were 127 corrections. But of -- significantly, of the 220 names, 140 were found in Srebrenica-related grave-sites by ICMP. So I think that concludes that we are not quite certain but every indication is that many of these dates were wrong. From the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless these persons, having died years before, were transported to the graves and then put there, which, I do understand is part of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's possible. I -- to me, as a layman in this, I would say that sounds unlikely but not impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We hear you as an expert so ... Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One follow-up question on this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, we are going beyond the one hour, but we have -- I would say a realistic expectation to conclude in five minutes and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And looking at Mr. Mladic, whether he wants to take the break or to continue for that five minutes. You can consult. Meanwhile. We'll stop immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, if he so chooses.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Dr. Brunborg, if you can look with me at -- and I'm going to go by the ICMP protocol number, it's the column that's the second from the right, and just past the half -- mid-point of the screen, we have the number 3238-03. It's a body that was recovered in Cerska and under clarification requests that it says, "Yes, but there is no corrected date of death and the date of death remains 10/01/1994." Would that indicate that the further inquiry from the armija BiH confirmed that the originally reported date of 10/01/1994 is still the date that they confirmed for this particular individual?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But we need to consult their response to the OTP from the request. But I'm glad that you now made me aware of the changes which were, say, at the bottom, the two -- the three, 10th of January, 1994, deaths have been changed to 12th of July, which I -- I oversaw that. And that is the case for many of the others. So the information is lacking here.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Agreed. And if we look at the four on the bottom for whom the dates have been changed, I can -- this is in B/C/S but it says next to at least three of them "Put Srebrenica-Tuzla," which would mean, of course, the road from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Looking at this information we cannot, therefore, exclude that these persons would have died in combat on the road from Srebrenica to Tuzla; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has always said that he doesn't know who died in combat or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He only commented on a wrong date. Therefore, that has been clarified. Now, if you think you can answer that question where you said many times before that you couldn't, please tell us why you can and then give the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further comments on that. I -- agree with you. I don't have any information on combat deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm done. Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you again, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour, for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then these questions by the Defence have triggered no -- and by the Bench have trigger no need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I just have the -- the report and the missing list that's offered into evidence now. The report was 11269 and the list was 11270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection. I thought there was one more document you used though. Let me just double-check, if I can. While I'm on my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While you're checking, I'll ask Madam Registrar to assign the numbers. 11269, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1900, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1900 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- receives P1901, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence under that number, but I take it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I have one more document that I had marked that you had used which was 65 ter 25879.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- yes, that is included -- that -- I just pulled that from the report and just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It combines, as a matter of fact, two diagrams, I think, and then in the third the same information is combined but the two diagrams -- at the same time, Mr. McCloskey, I think the third version is added. The third.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since questions have been asked about that third - how do you call that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Tables chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Table chart. Then perhaps it would be better for a better understanding by those following up, if there are any, to have that in evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think so. That should be 25879 and the other tame is 25878, both in the report but as you say referred to this way. So, yes, it's best to have it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. It keeps on saying 25789 instead of 25879.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 25879.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1902, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. And the other one was 25878.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1903, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1903 is admitted into evidence. Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd bear one minute with me. The Chamber, Mr. McCloskey, received today a filing under the name "Defence Motion to Enlarge Time to Respond to Prosecution Motion to Admit Evidence from the Bar Table, Excerpts from Mladic Audiotapes," and the Defence respectfully requests that the Trial Chamber grant an enlargement of an additional 14 days for the Defence to respond to the Prosecution's motion. And I think the response was due ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday. So two questions: First, do you have any problems that the request was -- no, it was filed -- yes, today. It's -- the date filed says 25th. Was it filed on the 25th? It was filed on the 25th. So within the time-limits. Any problem in giving the Defence 14 more days to respond to your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was informed about this. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in the absence of any objections, the Chamber grants the motion, the title of which I read out a minute ago, an enlargement of time of an additional 14 days for the Defence to respond to that motion. Hereby granted orally. Any other matter? Then, Mr. Brunborg, I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions. You are excused, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no other matters to be raised, which means that we'll adjourn until Monday, the 19th of August, 2013, in this same courtroom, III, at 9.30 in the morning. And I wish everyone, although under different circumstances, a good rest to the extent we are able to rest during the three weeks to come, and hope to see you back in good health on the 19th of August. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of August, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.51 a.m.,
